title: Personal Pronouns
grammarPoint: Polish personal pronouns: ja, ty, on, ona, ono, my, wy, oni, one

explanation.text:
Polish has nine personal pronouns covering singular and plural. Unlike English, they are often **omitted** in speech because verb endings show who the subject is. Use pronouns when you want to emphasise who is doing the action.

| | Singular | Plural |
|--|----------|--------|
| 1st | **ja** (I) | **my** (we) |
| 2nd | **ty** (you) | **wy** (you all) |
| 3rd m. | **on** (he) | **oni** (they — mixed/male) |
| 3rd f. | **ona** (she) | **one** (they — all female) |
| 3rd n. | **ono** (it) | **one** (they — neuter) |

In everyday speech: *Idę do sklepu* (not *Ja idę…*) is more natural.
notes: Pronouns are dropped in most sentences — the verb ending is enough.
Use ja/ty/on etc. for contrast or emphasis: 'Ja idę, ty zostajesz.'
oni = they (group with at least one male); one = they (all female or all neuter)
Pan (Mr) / Pani (Ms) are used instead of ty in formal address — covered in A2.

exercises.prompt: ___ jesteśmy z Polski. (We are from Poland.)

exercises.explanation: You heard: 'Ona jest z Warszawy.' — She is from Warsaw. 'Ona' = she, 'jest' = is, 'z Warszawy' = from Warsaw.

exercises.prompt: Build: He is a student. (Use the pronoun for emphasis.)
exercises.explanation: 'On jest studentem' = He is a student. On = he, jest = is (3rd sg.), studentem = instrumental of student.

exercises.prompt: Piotr i Marek są Polakami. What pronoun could replace 'Piotr i Marek'?
exercises.explanation: Piotr and Marek are two males, so the pronoun is 'oni' (they — mixed or male group).
